claim: Loss of Kiaa1024L/Minar2 caused deafness in mice.
source: Loss of Kiaa1024L/Minar2, a previously understudied gene, caused deafness in mice, but how it functioned in the hearing was unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Bowl et al., 2017; Ingham et al., 2019) as stated in the Introduction section.

claim: Disruption of kiaa1024L/minar2 causes hearing loss in zebrafish.
source: Here, we show that disruption of kiaa1024L/minar2 causes hearing loss in the zebrafish.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including C-start response rates and auditory evoked potential measurements shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Defects in mechanotransduction are observed in the kiaa1024L/minar2 mutant.
source: Defects in mechanotransduction, longer and thinner hair bundles, and enlarged apical lysosomes in hair cells are observed in the kiaa1024L/minar2 mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by AM1-43 labeling data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Hair bundles are longer and thinner in the kiaa1024L/minar2 mutant.
source: Defects in mechanotransduction, longer and thinner hair bundles, and enlarged apical lysosomes in hair cells are observed in the kiaa1024L/minar2 mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining and measurements shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Enlarged apical lysosomes in hair cells are observed in the kiaa1024L/minar2 mutant.
source: Defects in mechanotransduction, longer and thinner hair bundles, and enlarged apical lysosomes in hair cells are observed in the kiaa1024L/minar2 mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by Lamp1-GFP labeling data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Kiaa1024L/Minar2 is mainly localized to lysosomes in cultured cells.
source: In cultured cells, Kiaa1024L/Minar2 is mainly localized to lysosomes, and its overexpression recruits cholesterol and increases cholesterol labeling.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization experiments with lysosomal markers shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Overexpression of Kiaa1024L/Minar2 recruits cholesterol and increases cholesterol labeling.
source: In cultured cells, Kiaa1024L/Minar2 is mainly localized to lysosomes, and its overexpression recruits cholesterol and increases cholesterol labeling.
evidence: This claim is supported by filipin staining experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cholesterol is highly enriched in the hair bundle membrane.
source: Strikingly, cholesterol is highly enriched in the hair bundle membrane, and loss of kiaa1024L/minar2 reduces cholesterol localization to the hair bundles.
evidence: This claim is supported by D4H-mCherry probe distribution data shown in Figure 4A and quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of kiaa1024L/minar2 reduces cholesterol localization to the hair bundles.
source: Strikingly, cholesterol is highly enriched in the hair bundle membrane, and loss of kiaa1024L/minar2 reduces cholesterol localization to the hair bundles.
evidence: This claim is supported by D4H-mCherry intensity measurements in mutants shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Lowering cholesterol levels aggravates hair cell defects in the kiaa1024L/minar2 mutant.
source: Lowering cholesterol levels aggravates, while increasing cholesterol levels rescues the hair cell defects in the kiaa1024L/minar2 mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by 2HPβCD and U18666A treatment experiments shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Increasing cholesterol levels rescues the hair cell defects in the kiaa1024L/minar2 mutant.
source: Lowering cholesterol levels aggravates, while increasing cholesterol levels rescues the hair cell defects in the kiaa1024L/minar2 mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by efavirenz and voriconazole treatment experiments shown in Figure 6A-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cholesterol plays an essential role in hair bundles.
source: Therefore, cholesterol plays an essential role in hair bundles, and Kiaa1024L/Minar2 regulates cholesterol distribution and homeostasis to ensure normal hearing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of cholesterol distribution, mutant phenotypes, and pharmacological rescue experiments.

claim: Kiaa1024L/Minar2 regulates cholesterol distribution and homeostasis to ensure normal hearing.
source: Therefore, cholesterol plays an essential role in hair bundles, and Kiaa1024L/Minar2 regulates cholesterol distribution and homeostasis to ensure normal hearing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results showing Minar2 localization, cholesterol distribution changes in mutants, and rescue by cholesterol-modulating drugs.

claim: Hearing loss is one of the most common disabilities in humans.
source: Hearing loss is one of the most common disabilities in humans (World-Health-Organization, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to World Health Organization data.

claim: Over 120 genes essential for normal hearing have been identified through studies of genes linked to non-syndromic deafness.
source: Studies of genes linked to non-syndromic deafness have identified over 120 genes essential for normal hearing (Shearer et al., 1993; Van Camp and Smith, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Large-scale, unbiased genetic screens in mouse and zebrafish have identified multiple hearing loss genes.
source: Large-scale, unbiased genetic screens in the mouse (Bowl et al., 2017; Ingham et al., 2019) and the zebrafish (Whitfield et al., 1996) model systems have additionally identified multiple hearing loss genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published genetic screens.

claim: A number of phenotypically identified hearing loss genes are previously uncharacterized and have no demonstrated functional roles.
source: Interestingly, a number of these phenotypically identified hearing loss genes are previously uncharacterized and have no demonstrated functional roles, hinting that some biological processes required for normal auditory function have not been sufficiently explored (Bowl et al., 2017; Ingham et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genetic screen studies.

claim: Auditory hair cells are sensory receptor cells that convert acoustic and mechanical stimuli into electrical signals initiating hearing.
source: The auditory hair cells are the sensory receptor cells that convert acoustic and mechanical stimuli into electrical signals initiating hearing (Fettiplace, 2017; Hudspeth, 1989; Ó Maoiléidigh and Ricci, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on hair cell function.

claim: The hair bundle is a specialized organelle situated at the apical surface of each hair cell.
source: The hair bundle, a specialized organelle situated at the apical surface of each hair cell, responds to mechanical displacement in a direction-dependent manner (Flock, 1964; Tilney et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies on hair bundle structure.

claim: The hair bundle responds to mechanical displacement in a direction-dependent manner.
source: The hair bundle, a specialized organelle situated at the apical surface of each hair cell, responds to mechanical displacement in a direction-dependent manner (Flock, 1964; Tilney et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies on hair bundle function.

claim: The hair bundle is essential for mechanoelectrical transduction (MET).
source: The hair bundle is essential for mechanoelectrical transduction (MET), and defects in the hair bundle can cause hearing loss (Belyantseva et al., 2009; Blanco-Sánchez et al., 2014; Kozlov et al., 2007; Noben-Trauth et al., 2003; Perrin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies linking hair bundle defects to hearing loss.

claim: Defects in the hair bundle can cause hearing loss.
source: The hair bundle is essential for mechanoelectrical transduction (MET), and defects in the hair bundle can cause hearing loss (Belyantseva et al., 2009; Blanco-Sánchez et al., 2014; Kozlov et al., 2007; Noben-Trauth et al., 2003; Perrin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating this relationship.

claim: Several proteins are required for the morphogenesis and physiological regulation of the hair bundle.
source: Several proteins, such as adhesion molecules, actin-bundling proteins, and disease-associated proteins are required for the morphogenesis and physiological regulation of the hair bundle (Barr-Gillespie, 2015; Blanco-Sánchez et al., 2017; McGrath et al., 2017; Tilney et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on hair bundle proteins.

claim: Specific lipid molecules may play a role in the hair bundle.
source: In addition, specific lipid molecules may play a role in the hair bundle.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent examples of PIP2 function in hair bundles.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) is localized to hair bundles.
source: For instance, phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) is localized to hair bundles, and it binds to the MET channel component TMIE (Cunningham et al., 2020) and regulates the rates of fast and slow adaptation (Effertz et al., 2017; Hirono et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on PIP2 localization and function.

claim: PIP2 binds to the MET channel component TMIE.
source: For instance, phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) is localized to hair bundles, and it binds to the MET channel component TMIE (Cunningham et al., 2020) and regulates the rates of fast and slow adaptation (Effertz et al., 2017; Hirono et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cunningham et al., 2020.

claim: PIP2 regulates the rates of fast and slow adaptation in hair cells.
source: For instance, phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) is localized to hair bundles, and it binds to the MET channel component TMIE (Cunningham et al., 2020) and regulates the rates of fast and slow adaptation (Effertz et al., 2017; Hirono et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Effertz et al., 2017 and Hirono et al., 2004.

claim: Cholesterol is an important component of eukaryotic cell membranes.
source: Cholesterol is an important component of eukaryotic cell membranes, and it controls membrane stiffness, tension, fluidity, and other membrane properties (Maxfield and van Meer, 2010; Subczynski et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on cholesterol function.

claim: Cholesterol controls membrane stiffness, tension, fluidity, and other membrane properties.
source: Cholesterol is an important component of eukaryotic cell membranes, and it controls membrane stiffness, tension, fluidity, and other membrane properties (Maxfield and van Meer, 2010; Subczynski et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on cholesterol's effects on membrane properties.

claim: Cholesterol plays a regulatory function by interacting with membrane proteins.
source: Cholesterol also plays a regulatory function by interacting with membrane proteins (Harris, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Harris, 2010.

claim: Abnormally high or low cholesterol levels are detrimental to hearing.
source: Previous studies showed that abnormally high or low cholesterol levels are detrimental to hearing (Corwin and Warchol, 1991; Crumling et al., 2012; Ding et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2005; King et al., 2014a; King et al., 2014b; Morizono and Paparella, 1978; Sikora et al., 1986; Takahashi et al., 2016; Thoenes et al., 2015; Xing et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on cholesterol and hearing.

claim: Cholesterol is not uniformly distributed in hair cell membranes.
source: Early studies also showed that cholesterol is not uniformly distributed in the hair cell membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent citations to studies showing differential cholesterol distribution.

claim: The intensities of cholesterol labeling in hair cells are higher in the apical membranes compared to the lateral membranes.
source: The intensities of cholesterol labeling the hair cells were higher in the apical membranes when compared to those of the lateral membranes (Nguyen and Brownell, 1998; Takahashi et al., 2016), and freeze-fracture images of hair cells suggested that the stereocilia membrane was densely covered with cholesterol (Forge et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nguyen and Brownell, 1998 and Takahashi et al., 2016.

claim: Freeze-fracture images of hair cells suggest that the stereocilia membrane is densely covered with cholesterol.
source: The intensities of cholesterol labeling the hair cells were higher in the apical membranes when compared to those of the lateral membranes (Nguyen and Brownell, 1998; Takahashi et al., 2016), and freeze-fracture images of hair cells suggested that the stereocilia membrane was densely covered with cholesterol (Forge et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Forge et al., 1988.

claim: The distribution of cholesterol in hair cells in vivo is not well characterized.
source: Nevertheless, the distribution of cholesterol in hair cells in vivo, and cholesterol's functional role in hair cells are not well characterized.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the existing literature.

claim: Cholesterol's functional role in hair cells is not well characterized.
source: Nevertheless, the distribution of cholesterol in hair cells in vivo, and cholesterol's functional role in hair cells are not well characterized.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the existing literature.

claim: Kiaa1024L/Minar2 was identified in a hearing loss screen in mouse knockout strains using the auditory brainstem response test.
source: Kiaa1024L/Minar2, a previously understudied gene, was identified in a hearing loss screen in mouse knockout strains using the auditory brainstem response test.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bowl et al., 2017 and Ingham et al., 2019.

claim: Homozygous Kiaa1024L/Minar2 knockout mice aged 14 weeks old had severely raised ABR thresholds at all frequencies tested.
source: The homozygous Kiaa1024L/Minar2 knockout mice aged 14 weeks old had severely raised ABR thresholds at all frequencies tested (Bowl et al., 2017; Ingham et al., 2019), but how Kiaa1024L/Minar2 functioned in the hearing was unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bowl et al., 2017 and Ingham et al., 2019.

claim: kiaa1024L/minar2 is expressed in zebrafish mechanosensory hair cells.
source: Here we show kiaa1024L/minar2 is expressed in the zebrafish mechanosensory hair cells, and disruption of kiaa1024L/minar2 causes hearing loss in the zebrafish larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GFP or FLAG-tagged Kiaa1024L/Minar2 protein is distributed in the stereocilia and the apical endo-membranes.
source: We next show that GFP or FLAG-tagged Kiaa1024L/Minar2 protein is distributed in the stereocilia and the apical endo-membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Kiaa1024L/Minar2 protein is mainly localized to lysosomes in cultured cells.
source: In vitro studies in cultured cells show that the Kiaa1024L/Minar2 protein is mainly localized to lysosomes, and overexpression of Kiaa1024L/Minar2 recruits cholesterol and results in increased intracellular cholesterol levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Overexpression of Kiaa1024L/Minar2 recruits cholesterol and results in increased intracellular cholesterol levels.
source: In vitro studies in cultured cells show that the Kiaa1024L/Minar2 protein is mainly localized to lysosomes, and overexpression of Kiaa1024L/Minar2 recruits cholesterol and results in increased intracellular cholesterol levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by filipin staining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Drug treatment that lowers cholesterol levels aggravates hair cell defects and hearing in the mutant kiaa1024L/minar2 larvae.
source: Drug treatment that lowers cholesterol levels aggravates, whereas treatment that raises cholesterol levels rescues hair cell defects and hearing in the mutant kiaa1024L/minar2 larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by 2HPβCD and U18666A treatment data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Treatment that raises cholesterol levels rescues hair cell defects and hearing in the mutant kiaa1024L/minar2 larvae.
source: Drug treatment that lowers cholesterol levels aggravates, whereas treatment that raises cholesterol levels rescues hair cell defects and hearing in the mutant kiaa1024L/minar2 larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by efavirenz and voriconazole treatment data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kiaa1024L/minar2 gene orthologs are found in vertebrate species only.
source: Kiaa1024L/minar2 gene orthologs are found in vertebrate species only (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Kiaa1024L/minar2 belongs to the UPF0258 gene family, which also includes kiaa1024/minar1/ubtor.
source: It belongs to the UPF0258 gene family, which also includes kiaa1024/minar1/ubtor (Ho et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2018 and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: There are two kiaa1024/minar1/ubtor gene orthologs in the zebrafish genome.
source: Based on genome annotations and BLAST search results, there are two kiaa1024/minar1/ubtor gene orthologs (named ubtora and ubtorb in Zhang et al., 2018), and a single kiaa1024l/minar2 gene ortholog in the zebrafish genome.
evidence: This claim is based on genome annotation analysis and BLAST searches.

claim: There is a single kiaa1024l/minar2 gene ortholog in the zebrafish genome.
source: Based on genome annotations and BLAST search results, there are two kiaa1024/minar1/ubtor gene orthologs (named ubtora and ubtorb in Zhang et al., 2018), and a single kiaa1024l/minar2 gene ortholog in the zebrafish genome.
evidence: This claim is based on genome annotation analysis and BLAST searches.

claim: The transcripts of minar2 orthologs are highly enriched in the auditory hair cells of the mouse and the zebrafish.
source: We surveyed available sequencing data (Barta et al., 2018; Elkon et al., 2015; Erickson and Nicolson, 2015; Liu et al., 2018) and found the transcripts of minar2 orthologs were highly enriched in the auditory hair cells of the mouse and the zebrafish (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MINAR2 is specifically expressed in differentiated hair cells in a human inner ear organoid model.
source: In a human inner ear organoid model (Steinhart et al., 2022), MINAR2 is specifically expressed in differentiated hair cells, similar to known differentiated hair cell markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of data from Steinhart et al., 2022 shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mutation in the minar2fs139 allele is a 5 bp deletion in exon 1.
source: The mutation in the minar2fs139 allele was a 5 bp deletion in exon 1, and in the minar2fs140 allele was a 5 bp insertion in exon 1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The mutation in the minar2fs140 allele is a 5 bp insertion in exon 1.
source: The mutation in the minar2fs139 allele was a 5 bp deletion in exon 1, and in the minar2fs140 allele was a 5 bp insertion in exon 1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both minar2fs139 and minar2fs140 mutations are frameshift mutations that lead to premature termination of protein translation.
source: Both mutations were frameshift mutations and led to premature termination of protein translation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the nature of the mutations (5 bp deletion/insertion) and their effects on the reading frame.

claim: The mutant Minar2 proteins lack the transmembrane helix located at the carboxyl terminus.
source: The translatable protein sequence in either mutant was very short and lacked the transmembrane helix located at the carboxyl terminus of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the predicted protein sequences shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The mutant Minar2fs139 protein is predicted to translate to the 25th amino acid, then adds 28 code-shifted residues before the reading frame stops.
source: The mutant Minar2fs139 protein was predicted to translate to the 25th amino acid, then adds 28 code-shifted residues before the reading frame stopped.
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction of the mutant protein sequence.

claim: The mutant Minar2fs140 protein is predicted to translate to the 26th amino acid, then adds 55 code-shifted residues.
source: The mutant Minar2fs140 protein was predicted to translate to the 26th amino acid, then adds 55 code-shifted residues.
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction of the mutant protein sequence.

claim: Both minar2fs139 and minar2fs140 mutants are expected to be loss of function alleles.
source: Thus, both mutants were expected to be loss of function alleles.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the severe truncation of the predicted protein products.

claim: The expression levels of minar2 in the two mutants are markedly down-regulated in the developing zebrafish.
source: In addition, quantitative PCR analyses showed the expression levels of minar2 in the two mutants were markedly down-regulated in the developing zebrafish, most likely because the premature translational terminations activated the nonsense-mediated mRNA decays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The premature translational terminations likely activated nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.
source: In addition, quantitative PCR analyses showed the expression levels of minar2 in the two mutants were markedly down-regulated in the developing zebrafish, most likely because the premature translational terminations activated the nonsense-mediated mRNA decays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed mRNA down-regulation and known mechanisms of nonsense-mediated decay.

claim: Expression levels of ubtora/minar1a and ubtorb/minar1b are not changed in the minar2fs139 nor the minar2fs140 mutants.
source: To assess if loss of minar2 resulted in genetic compensation (El-Brolosy et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019) by upregulating kiaa1024/ubtor/minar1 gene expression, we carried out quantitative PCR and found that expression levels of ubtora/minar1a and ubtorb/minar1b were not changed in the minar2fs139 nor the minar2fs140 mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The SLC response rates to a 200 Hz stimulus are significantly reduced in the minar2fs139 mutant at 8 dpf.
source: We found the SLC response rates to a 200 Hz stimulus were significantly reduced in the minar2fs139 mutant at 8 dpf (Figure 1B, median response rates: 80% in the wild type, and 60% in the mutant. P<0.0001, Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This claim is supported by C-start response data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The minar2fs139 mutant has significantly elevated AEP thresholds compared with the wild type control.
source: Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA revealed that the minar2fs139 mutant had significantly elevated AEP thresholds compared with the wild type control (For genotype factor, F(1, 22)=7.457, p=0.0122. For genotype x frequency, F(5, 110)=6.072, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by AEP recording data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The AEP thresholds are significantly higher at 100–400 Hz tone bursts in the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: The AEP thresholds were significantly higher at 100–400 Hz tone bursts in the minar2fs139 mutant (for 100 Hz tone, 151.0±1.2 dB for minar2fs139, 145.7±1.4 dB for wild type control; for 200 Hz tone, 152.2±1.1 dB for minar2fs139, 145.2±2.0 dB for wild type control; for 400 Hz, 143.6±1.1 dB for minar2fs139, 138.6±1.3 dB for wild type control).
evidence: This claim is supported by AEP recording data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: minar2 is required for normal hearing in zebrafish larvae.
source: These results indicate that minar2 is required for normal hearing in the zebrafish larvae, and together with the loss of hearing phenotype in Minar2 knockout mice (Bowl et al., 2017; Ingham et al., 2019), strengthen the conclusion that minar2 orthologs play essential roles in the auditory functions of the vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by the C-start and AEP data presented in Figure 1B-C.

claim: minar2 orthologs play essential roles in the auditory functions of vertebrates.
source: These results indicate that minar2 is required for normal hearing in the zebrafish larvae, and together with the loss of hearing phenotype in Minar2 knockout mice (Bowl et al., 2017; Ingham et al., 2019), strengthen the conclusion that minar2 orthologs play essential roles in the auditory functions of the vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined evidence in zebrafish and mice.

claim: The labeling intensities of AM1-43 are markedly reduced in the hair cells of the lateral line neuromasts of the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: We found the labeling intensities of AM1-43 were markedly reduced in the hair cells of the lateral line neuromasts of the minar2fs139 mutant (56.8% and 51.1% of wild-type controls at 5 dpf and 8 dpf, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by AM1-43 labeling data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The average number of hair cells is decreased in the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: The results showed the average number of hair cells was decreased in the minar2fs139 mutant (82.3% and 82.1% of wild-type controls at 5 dpf and 8 dpf, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by hair cell counting data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Loss of minar2 function mainly affects hair cell mechanotransduction in zebrafish larvae.
source: Because the decreases in hair cell numbers (~18% reduction) are smaller than those reductions of AM1-43 labeling intensities (~50% reduction), these results suggest that loss of minar2 function mainly affects hair cell mechanotransduction in the zebrafish larvae.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparing the magnitude of hair cell loss versus AM1-43 labeling reduction.

claim: Loss of minar2 does not alter the number of hair cells in the inner ears of zebrafish larvae.
source: In the zebrafish larvae, loss of minar2 didn't alter the number of hair cells in the inner ears (for 5 dpf wild type: 23.9±0.6, minar2fs139 mutant: 23.6±0.4, minar2fs140 mutant: 24.9±0.6 hair cells, F(2, 82)=1.399, p=0.253; for 8 dpf wild type: 32.5±0.7, minar2fs139 mutant: 32.9±0.5, minar2fs140 mutant: 33.0±0.7 hair cells, F(2, 79)=0.2378, p=0.789, both of the lateral crista of inner ear, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by hair cell counting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The homozygous minar2 mutants are viable.
source: The homozygous minar2 mutants were viable, and the body length and body weight of adults were no different from the wild-type controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation and measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The body length and body weight of adult minar2 mutants are no different from wild-type controls.
source: The homozygous minar2 mutants were viable, and the body length and body weight of adults were no different from the wild-type controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The inner ear regions are smaller in the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: Nevertheless, hematoxylin and eosin staining of head sections suggested the inner ear regions were smaller and the numbers of hair cells were decreased in the utricle, semicircular canal crista, and saccule of the minar2fs139 mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The numbers of hair cells are decreased in the utricle, semicircular canal crista, and saccule of the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: Nevertheless, hematoxylin and eosin staining of head sections suggested the inner ear regions were smaller and the numbers of hair cells were decreased in the utricle, semicircular canal crista, and saccule of the minar2fs139 mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The average numbers of hair cells are broadly decreased across different regions of utricles and saccules in the minar2fs139 mutant, ranging from 71.2% to 84.3% of wild-type controls.
source: The average numbers of hair cells were broadly decreased across different regions of utricles and saccules in the minar2fs139 mutant, ranging from 71.2% to 84.3% of wild-type controls (Figure 1F, for the utricles, the genotype factor, F(1, 32)=37.77, p<0.0001; for the saccules, the genotype factor, F(1, 19)=19.94, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by hair cell counting data in dissected inner ear organs shown in Figure 1F.

claim: minar2 is required for mechanotransduction in zebrafish larvae.
source: We conclude that minar2 is required for mechanotransduction in the zebrafish larvae, and loss of minar2 reduces the number of inner ear hair cells in the zebrafish adults.
evidence: This claim is supported by AM1-43 labeling data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Loss of minar2 reduces the number of inner ear hair cells in zebrafish adults.
source: We conclude that minar2 is required for mechanotransduction in the zebrafish larvae, and loss of minar2 reduces the number of inner ear hair cells in the zebrafish adults.
evidence: This claim is supported by hair cell counting data in adult zebrafish shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GFP-Minar2 is localized to the stereocilia and the apical region of the hair cell.
source: We observed that GFP-Minar2 was localized to the stereocilia and the apical region of the hair cell, apparently around and just below the cuticular plate.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The GFP-Minar2 fluorescence co-localizes with phalloidin-labeled stereocilia.
source: The GFP-Minar2 fluorescence co-localized with the phalloidin-labeled stereocilia (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization imaging shown in Figure 2A.

claim: FLAG-Minar2 is localized to the stereocilia and the apical region of hair cells.
source: The results showed that FLAG-Minar2 was similarly localized to the stereocilia and the apical region of hair cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GFP-Minar2 is localized to the stereocilia and the apical region of hair cells in the stable transgenic line.
source: We subsequently generated a stable transgenic line using the myo6b:GFP-Minar2 construct and we found that GFP-Minar2 was also localized to the stereocilia and the apical region of the hair cells in the transgenic animals (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data from the transgenic line shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Prominent vesicle-like structures are seen below the cuticular plate in GFP-Minar2 expressing cells.
source: Prominent vesicle-like structures were seen below the cuticular plate, while a ring-like structure was often observed at the base of the hair bundle.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of GFP-Minar2 distribution shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A ring-like structure is often observed at the base of the hair bundle in GFP-Minar2 expressing cells.
source: Prominent vesicle-like structures were seen below the cuticular plate, while a ring-like structure was often observed at the base of the hair bundle.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of GFP-Minar2 distribution shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is no observable GFP-Minar2 signal in the kinocilia.
source: We co-labeled the kinocilia with anti-acetylated tubulin antibodies in the myo6b:GFP-Minar2 transgenic zebrafish and found there was no observable GFP-Minar2 signal in the kinocilia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-labeling experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Hair bundles of inner ear hair cells are longer in the mutant minar2fs139 and minar2fs140 larvae.
source: We labeled the hair bundles with phalloidin and observed that the hair bundles of inner ear hair cells were longer in the mutant minar2fs139 and minar2fs140 larvae (Figure 2C, for 5 dpf, wt: 4.77±0.06 μm, minar2fs139: 5.62±0.07 μm, minar2fs140: 5.15±0.07 μm, F(2, 847)=42.58, p<0.001; for 8 dpf, wt: 5.72±0.08 μm, minar2fs139: 6.80±0.09 μm, minar2fs140: 6.10±0.08 μm, F(2, 817)=42.95, p<0.001), and the hair bundles also appeared thinner.
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining and measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Hair bundles appear thinner in the mutant minar2fs139 and minar2fs140 larvae.
source: We labeled the hair bundles with phalloidin and observed that the hair bundles of inner ear hair cells were longer in the mutant minar2fs139 and minar2fs140 larvae (Figure 2C, for 5 dpf, wt: 4.77±0.06 μm, minar2fs139: 5.62±0.07 μm, minar2fs140: 5.15±0.07 μm, F(2, 847)=42.58, p<0.001; for 8 dpf, wt: 5.72±0.08 μm, minar2fs139: 6.80±0.09 μm, minar2fs140: 6.10±0.08 μm, F(2, 817)=42.95, p<0.001), and the hair bundles also appeared thinner.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of phalloidin-stained hair bundles shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The thinning and lengthening of mutant hair bundles are more pronounced in adult minar2fs139 mutants.
source: The thinning and lengthening of the mutant hair bundles were more pronounced in adult minar2fs139 mutants (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements in adult zebrafish shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In 6-month-old adults, the average length of mutant hair bundles is more than 50% longer than that of wild type controls.
source: In the 6-month-old adults, the average length of mutant hair bundles was more than 50% longer than that of wild type controls (wt: 3.77±0.11 μm, minar2fs139: 5.77±0.12 μm, t=12.05, df = 158, p<0.0001), and the width was only half that of the controls (wt: 1.66±0.05 μm, minar2fs139: 0.88±0.04 μm, t=12.65, df = 158, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In 6-month-old adults, the width of mutant hair bundles is only half that of wild type controls.
source: In the 6-month-old adults, the average length of mutant hair bundles was more than 50% longer than that of wild type controls (wt: 3.77±0.11 μm, minar2fs139: 5.77±0.12 μm, t=12.05, df = 158, p<0.0001), and the width was only half that of the controls (wt: 1.66±0.05 μm, minar2fs139: 0.88±0.04 μm, t=12.65, df = 158, p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The kinocilia of lateral line hair cells are disorganized in the minar2 mutant larvae.
source: We also found that the kinocilia of lateral line hair cells were disorganized in the minar2 mutant larvae, in contrast to the normal bundled together morphology in the wild-type animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, for 5 dpf, minar2fs139: p<0.001, minar2fs140: p<0.01; for 8 dpf, minar2fs139: p<0.001, minar2fs140: p<0.01. Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The apical region of the hair cell is teeming with endocytotic vesicles, many of which are lysosomes.
source: Previous electron microscopy and immunofluorescence microscopy studies showed that the apical region of the hair cell is teeming with endocytotic vesicles, many of which are lysosomes (Revelo et al., 2014; Spicer et al., 1999; Wiwatpanit et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lamp1-GFP-positive lysosomes are abundantly distributed in the apical region of inner ear hair cells.
source: Similar to the findings in the mouse model, we observed that Lamp1-GFP-positive lysosomes were abundantly distributed in the apical region of the inner ear hair cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Lamp1-GFP imaging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There are a few lysosomes distributed along the basolateral membrane of hair cells.
source: There were also a few lysosomes distributed along the basolateral membrane of the hair cells.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of Lamp1-GFP distribution shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In wild-type controls, most Lamp1-GFP labeled lysosomes are small sphere- or rod-shaped vesicles.
source: In the wild-type controls, most of these Lamp1-GFP labeled lysosomes were small sphere- or rod-shaped vesicles.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of Lamp1-GFP distribution shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Large-sized Lamp1-GFP-labeled structures are occasionally observed in wild-type controls (in 39 out of 184 hair cells).
source: Occasionally, rare and large-sized Lamp1-GFP-labeled structures were observed (in 39 out of 184 hair cells) and these structures likely were abnormally enlarged lysosomes or lysosome aggregates (diameter >2 μm).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of Lamp1-GFP structures shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Large round-shaped lysosomal structures (diameter >2 μm) are frequently observed in the inner ear hair cells of the minar2fs139 mutant (observed in 134 out of 236 hair cells).
source: In contrast, in the inner ear hair cells of the minar2fs139 mutant, the large round-shaped lysosomal structures (diameter >2 μm) were frequently observed (observed in 134 out of 236 hair cells), and these abnormally enlarged lysosome aggregates were always located at the apical region of the hair cells (Figure 2E, p<0.0001, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Abnormally enlarged lysosome aggregates are always located at the apical region of hair cells in the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: In contrast, in the inner ear hair cells of the minar2fs139 mutant, the large round-shaped lysosomal structures (diameter >2 μm) were frequently observed (observed in 134 out of 236 hair cells), and these abnormally enlarged lysosome aggregates were always located at the apical region of the hair cells (Figure 2E, p<0.0001, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of Lamp1-GFP distribution shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Abnormally enlarged lysosome aggregates are also observed in the hair cells of lateral line neuromasts in the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: Similar results showing abnormally enlarged lysosome aggregates were also observed in the hair cells of the lateral line neuromasts (Figure 2F, p<0.0001, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Minar2 may play a role in regulating the apical lysosomes in hair cells.
source: These data suggested that Minar2 may play a role in regulating the apical lysosomes in the hair cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of enlarged lysosomes in the minar2 mutant.

claim: GFP-Minar2 signals partially overlap with Lamp1-mCherry signals at the apical region of inner ear hair cells.
source: Consistent with this view, GFP-Minar2 signals partially overlapped with the Lamp1-mCherry signals at the apical region of the inner ear hair cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GFP-Minar2 most strongly co-localizes with lysosomes in cultured cells.
source: We found GFP-Minar2 most strongly co-localized with lysosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization experiments with organelle markers shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: When the morphology and distribution of lysosomes are altered after U18666A treatment, GFP-Minar2 signals follow the changes of lysosomes.
source: Furthermore, when the morphology and distribution of the lysosomes were altered after treatment with U18666A, GFP-Minar2 signals followed the changes of lysosomes, increased in the particle sizes, and accumulated toward the nuclear region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging after U18666A treatment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: GFP-Minar2 is localized on the lysosomal membranes.
source: We further stained the lysosome lumen with filipin staining of cholesterol, which was trapped inside the lysosome after treatment with U18666A; and we observed that GFP-Minar2 signals appeared as circles that circumscribed the filipin signals, indicating GFP-Minar2 was localized on the lysosomal membranes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-staining experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: A conserved sequence pattern in Minar2 matches the caveolin scaffolding domain (CSD).
source: One of the conserved sequence patterns (π-S/T-Ω-S/T-Ψ-ζ-ζ-Ω) had 125 hits in the Metazoa [taxid:33208] proteins, and 37 out of the 125 hit sequences matched to Caveolin-1 protein from various species (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein pattern search results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The matched sequence pattern resides in the caveolin scaffolding domain (CSD).
source: A close inspection revealed that the matched sequence pattern resided in the caveolin scaffolding domain (CSD), which is known to interact with other proteins (Murata et al., 1995; Razani et al., 2002) and lipid membranes (Schlegel et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and citations to studies on CSD function.

claim: The CSD of caveolin is known to interact with other proteins.
source: A close inspection revealed that the matched sequence pattern resided in the caveolin scaffolding domain (CSD), which is known to interact with other proteins (Murata et al., 1995; Razani et al., 2002) and lipid membranes (Schlegel et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murata et al., 1995 and Razani et al., 2002.

claim: The CSD of caveolin is known to interact with lipid membranes.
source: A close inspection revealed that the matched sequence pattern resided in the caveolin scaffolding domain (CSD), which is known to interact with other proteins (Murata et al., 1995; Razani et al., 2002) and lipid membranes (Schlegel et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schlegel et al., 1999.

claim: The CSD of caveolin directly binds to cholesterol in membranes.
source: The CSD of caveolin also directly binds to cholesterol in the membranes (Ikonen et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2016; Murata et al., 1995) and this binding may contribute to the enrichment of cholesterol in the caveolae (Everson and Smart, 2005; Frank et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on caveolin-cholesterol binding.

claim: CSD binding to cholesterol may contribute to the enrichment of cholesterol in caveolae.
source: The CSD of caveolin also directly binds to cholesterol in the membranes (Ikonen et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2016; Murata et al., 1995) and this binding may contribute to the enrichment of cholesterol in the caveolae (Everson and Smart, 2005; Frank et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Everson and Smart, 2005 and Frank et al., 2006.

claim: In cells expressing GFP-Minar2, filipin signals are accumulated in the perinuclear regions.
source: In contrast, in cells expressing GFP-Minar2 fusion protein, the filipin signals were accumulated in the perinuclear regions and there were strong overlaps between the Minar2 and the filipin signals in the perinuclear regions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by filipin staining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There are strong overlaps between Minar2 and filipin signals in the perinuclear regions.
source: In contrast, in cells expressing GFP-Minar2 fusion protein, the filipin signals were accumulated in the perinuclear regions and there were strong overlaps between the Minar2 and the filipin signals in the perinuclear regions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by filipin staining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There are significant increases of intracellular unesterified cholesterol in cells expressing GFP-Minar2.
source: Quantification of the filipin signals revealed that there were significant increases of intracellular unesterified cholesterol in cells expressing GFP-Minar2 (total filipin fluorescence, for HEK293 cells, 79.0±3.0 au for GFP-only control, 106±3.8 au for GFP-Minar2 group, t=5.654, df = 104.6, p<0.0001; for Cos-7 cells, 100.5±8.2 au for GFP-only control, 140.3±12.9 au for GFP-Minar2 group, t=2.608, df = 55.73, p=0.012).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of filipin staining shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GFP-Minar2 recruits filipin signals to where GFP signals are located.
source: The quantification results also confirmed that GFP-Minar2 recruited the filipin signals to where GFP signals were located (recruited filipin intensity, for HEK293 cells, 5.85±0.51 au for GFP-only control, 23.56±1.36 au for GFP-Minar2 group, t=12.20, df = 72.42, p<0.0001; for Cos-7 cells, 12.08±1.1 au for GFP-only control, 22.14±2.31 au for GFP-Minar2 group, t=3.903, df = 48.96, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of filipin recruitment shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cholesterol in biological membranes is organized in three pools: a fixed pool for membrane integrity, a sequestered pool with low chemical activity, and an active/accessible pool with high activity.
source: Previous studies suggested that cholesterol in the biological membranes is organized in three pools, a fixed pool for membrane integrity, a sequestered pool with low chemical activity, and an active/accessible pool with high activity (Das et al., 2014; Lange and Steck, 2016; Lange et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on cholesterol organization.

claim: Protein probes derived from Perfringolysin O (PFO) and the D4 domain have been widely used to measure the accessible pool of cholesterol in biological membranes.
source: Protein probes derived from the bacterial toxin Perfringolysin O (PFO) and the minimal cholesterol-binding domain 4 (D4 or D4H) of PFO have been widely used to measure the accessible pool of cholesterol in biological membranes (Das et al., 2014; Lim et al., 2019; Maekawa and Fairn, 2015; Naito et al., 2019; Schoop et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using D4H probes.

claim: GFP-Minar2 co-localizes with D4H-mCherry signals in cultured cells.
source: Similar to what was observed in cells stained by filipin, GFP-Minar2 co-localized with D4H-mCherry signals, and recruited the D4H-mCherry signals to the perinuclear regions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization imaging shown in Figure 3C.

claim: GFP-Minar2 recruits D4H-mCherry signals to the perinuclear regions.
source: Similar to what was observed in cells stained by filipin, GFP-Minar2 co-localized with D4H-mCherry signals, and recruited the D4H-mCherry signals to the perinuclear regions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Minar2 co-localizes with cholesterol.
source: We conclude that Minar2 co-localizes with cholesterol and that Minar2 may increase intracellular cholesterol levels when overexpressed in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data with filipin and D4H-mCherry shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Minar2 may increase intracellular cholesterol levels when overexpressed in vitro.
source: We conclude that Minar2 co-localizes with cholesterol and that Minar2 may increase intracellular cholesterol levels when overexpressed in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by filipin quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cholesterol levels are higher in the apical membranes than in the lateral wall membranes in isolated outer hair cells and fixed cochlear tissues.
source: In isolated outer hair cells and outer hair cells in fixed cochlear tissues, cholesterol levels are higher in the apical membranes than those in the lateral wall membranes (Nguyen and Brownell, 1998; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nguyen and Brownell, 1998 and Takahashi et al., 2016.

claim: The apical regions of inner ear hair cells show distinct filipin labeling.
source: The apical regions of inner ear hair cells showed distinct filipin labeling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by filipin staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: D4H-mCherry specifically labels the stereocilia when expressed in inner ear hair cells.
source: Strikingly, when expressed in the inner ear hair cells by microinjection, D4H-mCherry specifically labeled the stereocilia regardless of its expression levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Low-intensity labeling of kinocilia is observed in cells with high levels of D4H-mCherry expression.
source: Low-intensity labeling of kinocilia was also observed in cells with high levels of D4H-mCherry expression, while the basolateral membranes of hair cells were not or only very faintly labeled (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of D4H-mCherry distribution shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The basolateral membranes of hair cells are not or only very faintly labeled by D4H-mCherry.
source: Low-intensity labeling of kinocilia was also observed in cells with high levels of D4H-mCherry expression, while the basolateral membranes of hair cells were not or only very faintly labeled (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of D4H-mCherry distribution shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PM-GFP uniformly labels the basolateral membranes, stereocilia, and kinocilia membranes.
source: As expected, PM-GFP uniformly labeled the basolateral membranes, together with the stereocilia and the kinocilia membranes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The mean area of the stereocilium region is only 16.5 ± 0.1% of that of basolateral regions.
source: The results showed that although the mean area of the stereocilium region was only 16.5 ± 0.1% of that of basolateral regions, the mean PM-GFP fluorescence within the stereocilium regions was 73.7 ± 4.0% of that of the basolateral regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mean PM-GFP fluorescence within the stereocilium regions is 73.7 ± 4.0% of that of the basolateral regions.
source: The results showed that although the mean area of the stereocilium region was only 16.5 ± 0.1% of that of basolateral regions, the mean PM-GFP fluorescence within the stereocilium regions was 73.7 ± 4.0% of that of the basolateral regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mean D4H-mCherry fluorescence within the stereocilium regions is 567.7 ± 80.1% of that of the basolateral regions.
source: Strikingly, the mean D4H-mCherry fluorescence within the stereocilium regions was 567.7 ± 80.1% of that of the basolateral regions, which was 7.7 times higher than that of PM-GFP (p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is an enrichment of D4H-mCherry in the stereocilium membrane over the basolateral membranes.
source: Therefore, the disproportional distribution of D4H-mCherry in the stereocilium is much larger than what is expected from the distribution of the general plasma membrane probe PM-GFP, indicating that there was an enrichment of D4H-mCherry in the stereocilium membrane over the basolateral membranes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparing D4H-mCherry and PM-GFP distributions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The D4HT490G-L491G variant does not bind cholesterol.
source: Previous studies have shown that the threonine–leucine pair in loop L1 of PFO domain 4 is essential for cholesterol recognition, and substitution of the T490-L491 pair with glycine residues abolishes cholesterol binding without perturbation of the overall structure of PFO (Farrand et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Farrand et al., 2010.

claim: D4HT490G-L491G-mCherry gives rise to diffused signals in the cytoplasm only when expressed in hair cells.
source: When the D4HT490G-L491G-mCherry variant was expressed in the hair cells, it gave rise to diffused signals in the cytoplasm only (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: D4H-mCherry labels stereocilia in lateral line neuromast hair cells.
source: In the hair cells of the lateral line neuromasts, the stereocilia were similarly strongly labeled by D4H-mCherry.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There are observable but weaker D4H-mCherry signals on the basolateral membranes of lateral line hair cells.
source: There were also observable but weaker D4H-mCherry signals on the basolateral membranes of the lateral line hair cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of D4H-mCherry distribution shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There are high levels of cholesterol located in the stereocilia membranes.
source: These data suggested that there are high levels of cholesterol located in the stereocilia membranes, while the cholesterol levels are markedly lower in the basolateral membranes of the hair cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from D4H-mCherry distribution data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cholesterol levels are markedly lower in the basolateral membranes of hair cells.
source: These data suggested that there are high levels of cholesterol located in the stereocilia membranes, while the cholesterol levels are markedly lower in the basolateral membranes of the hair cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from D4H-mCherry distribution data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both GFP-Minar2 and D4H-mCherry signals co-localize in the stereocilia.
source: As expected, both GFP-Minar2 and D4H-mCherry signals co-localized in the stereocilia (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization imaging shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There are abundant GFP-Minar2 signals just below the stereocilia and in the apical region of hair cells.
source: Just below the stereocilia and in the apical region of hair cells, there were abundant GFP-Minar2 signals, and close inspections revealed a few D4H-mCherry-labeled structures that co-localized with GFP-Minar2 (Figure 4C insert).
evidence: This claim is based on observation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A few D4H-mCherry-labeled structures co-localize with GFP-Minar2 in the apical region.
source: Just below the stereocilia and in the apical region of hair cells, there were abundant GFP-Minar2 signals, and close inspections revealed a few D4H-mCherry-labeled structures that co-localized with GFP-Minar2 (Figure 4C insert).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging shown in Figure 4C insert.

claim: D4H-mCherry additionally labels kinocilia, in which GFP-Minar2 signals are absent.
source: D4H-mCherry additionally labeled kinocilia, in which GFP-Minar2 signals were absent.
evidence: This claim is based on observation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Minar2 co-localizes with cholesterol in the stereocilia in vivo.
source: Thus, similar to co-localization results in the cultured cells in vitro (Figure 3C), Minar2 co-localized with cholesterol in the stereocilia in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: D4H-mCherry still labels stereocilia in the hair cells of inner ears in the mutant minar2fs139 larvae.
source: In the hair cells of the inner ears in the mutant minar2fs139 larvae, D4H-mCherry still labeled stereocilia (Figure 4D), but the intensities of the signals were dramatically reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The intensities of D4H-mCherry signals are dramatically reduced in the mutant minar2fs139 larvae.
source: In the hair cells of the inner ears in the mutant minar2fs139 larvae, D4H-mCherry still labeled stereocilia (Figure 4D), but the intensities of the signals were dramatically reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The average D4H-mCherry signals of inner ear stereocilia in the minar2fs139 larvae are about half of those in wild controls.
source: The results showed the average D4H-mCherry signals of inner ear stereocilia in the minar2fs139 larvae were about half of those in the wild controls (59.16 ± 5.92% and 56.62 ± 7.15% for 5 and 8 dpf, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The expression levels of D4H-mCherry are similar between wild-type controls and mutant minar2fs139 larvae.
source: The decreases were not due to changes in transgene expression either, since the western blotting results showed that the expression levels of D4H-mCherry were similar between the wild-type controls and the mutant minar2fs139 larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a similar reduction of D4H-mCherry signal in lateral line neuromast hair cells at 5 dpf.
source: In the hair cells of lateral line neuromasts, there was a similar reduction of D4H-mCherry signal at 5 dpf (59.30 ± 5.98% of controls), while the signal intensity was no different from the wild-type controls at 8 dpf (121.39% of controls, n=41 and 44 for the wild type and the minar2fs139 mutant, respectively. t=0.8889, df = 83, p=0.3766).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4E.

claim: D4H-mCherry signal intensity is no different from wild-type controls at 8 dpf in lateral line neuromast hair cells.
source: In the hair cells of lateral line neuromasts, there was a similar reduction of D4H-mCherry signal at 5 dpf (59.30 ± 5.98% of controls), while the signal intensity was no different from the wild-type controls at 8 dpf (121.39% of controls, n=41 and 44 for the wild type and the minar2fs139 mutant, respectively. t=0.8889, df = 83, p=0.3766).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4E.

claim: D4H-mCherry labels many large, round- and rod-shaped vesicles in the cell body regions of neuromast hair cells in the minar2fs139 mutant at 8 dpf.
source: While D4H-mCherry primarily labeled the stereocilia membranes in both wild-type controls and the minar2fs139 mutant at 5 dpf, D4H-mCherry labeled many large, round- and rod-shaped vesicles in the cell body regions of the neuromast hair cells in the minar2fs139 mutant at 8 dpf (Figure 4E, p<0.01, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4E.

claim: D4H-mCherry-labeled large vesicles in the hair cells of minar2fs139 mutant likely correspond to enlarged lysosomes.
source: These D4H-mCherry-labeled large vesicles in the hair cells of minar2fs139 mutant likely corresponded to enlarged lysosomes, as these abnormal vesicles were co-labeled by the lysosome probe Lamp1-GFP, but not by the plasma membrane probe PM-GFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from co-labeling experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There are significant increases in relative mRNA expression for Srebp2 target genes hmgcr and hmgcs1 in the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: We found that there were significant increases in relative mRNA expression for Srebp2 target genes hmgcr (2.6±0.2 fold) and hmgcs1 (1.7±0.2 fold) in the minar2fs139 mutant, while expression levels of LXR target gene abcg1 and mylip were not changed (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Expression levels of LXR target genes abcg1 and mylip are not changed in the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: We found that there were significant increases in relative mRNA expression for Srebp2 target genes hmgcr (2.6±0.2 fold) and hmgcs1 (1.7±0.2 fold) in the minar2fs139 mutant, while expression levels of LXR target gene abcg1 and mylip were not changed (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The sterol synthesis pathway is activated due to a reduction of the accessible cholesterol pool in the minar2fs139 mutant larvae.
source: These results suggested that the sterol synthesis pathway was activated due to a reduction of the accessible cholesterol pool in the minar2fs139 mutant larvae.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the upregulation of Srebp2 target genes shown in Figure 4F.

claim: minar2 is required for normal cholesterol distribution and homeostasis in hair cells.
source: We conclude that minar2 is required for normal cholesterol distribution and homeostasis in the hair cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of D4H-mCherry distribution and gene expression changes.

claim: Treatment with 2HPβCD markedly decreases D4H-mCherry signals in neuromast hair cells.
source: As expected, treatment with 2HPβCD markedly decreased D4H-mCherry signals in the neuromast hair cells, indicating the cholesterol levels were reduced (16.5 ± 2.4% of those of control, Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The AM1-43 labeling intensities are significantly reduced after 2HPβCD treatment.
source: Moreover, the AM1-43 labeling intensities were significantly reduced after the 2HPβCD treatment (33.5% of those of controls), indicating the mechanotransduction was compromised when intracellular cholesterol was extracted (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mechanotransduction is compromised when intracellular cholesterol is extracted.
source: Moreover, the AM1-43 labeling intensities were significantly reduced after the 2HPβCD treatment (33.5% of those of controls), indicating the mechanotransduction was compromised when intracellular cholesterol was extracted (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the reduction in AM1-43 labeling after 2HPβCD treatment shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When minar2fs139 mutants are treated with 2HPβCD, the cholesterol levels in the hair bundles and the AM1-43 labeling intensities are further reduced to levels in the 2HPβCD-treated wild-type controls.
source: When the minar2fs139 mutants were treated with 2HPβCD, the cholesterol levels in the hair bundles and the AM1-43 labeling intensities were further reduced to levels in the 2HPβCD-treated wild-type controls (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: 2HPβCD treatment greatly compromises hearing in wild-type larvae.
source: Examination of the short-latency C-start response showed that 2HPβCD treatment had similar effects as it did on the AM1-43 labeling. It greatly compromised hearing in the wild-type larvae, and reduced hearing further in the minar2fs139 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by C-start response data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 2HPβCD treatment reduces hearing further in the minar2fs139 mutants.
source: Examination of the short-latency C-start response showed that 2HPβCD treatment had similar effects as it did on the AM1-43 labeling. It greatly compromised hearing in the wild-type larvae, and reduced hearing further in the minar2fs139 mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by C-start response data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Decreasing cholesterol levels in hair cells by 2HPβCD mimics the defects in the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: These data indicated that decreasing cholesterol levels in hair cells by 2HPβCD mimicked the defects in the minar2fs139 mutant.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar effects of 2HPβCD treatment and minar2 mutation shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: 2HPβCD treatment aggravates hair cell defects in the minar2fs139 mutant.
source: In addition, 2HPβCD treatment aggravated hair cell defects in the minar2fs139 mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by the additive effects shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Treatment with U18666A causes a strong accumulation of cholesterol in the lysosome lumen in cultured cells.
source: Unlike a general reduction of cholesterol levels after 2HPβCD treatment, treatment with U18666A caused a strong accumulation of cholesterol in the lysosome lumen in cultured cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by filipin staining after U18666A treatment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The D4H-mCherry labeling intensities are significantly decreased after U18666A treatment.
source: Nevertheless, the D4H-mCherry labeling intensities were significantly decreased after the U18666A treatment (50.2 ± 4.6% of those of control, Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5C.

claim: U18666A treatment alters the distribution of D4H-mCherry signals and gives rise to D4H-mCherry-labeled endo-membrane particles at basolateral regions in hair cells.
source: Treatment with U18666A also altered the distribution of the D4H-mCherry signals and gave rise to D4H-mCherry-labeled endo-membrane particles at basolateral regions in the hair cells (Figure 5C, figure insert).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging shown in Figure 5C insert.

claim: U18666A treatment strongly decreases the intensities of AM1-43 labeling.
source: Similar to the 2HPβCD treatment group, U18666A treatment strongly decreased the intensities of AM1-43 labeling, to levels similar in the 2HPβCD treatment group (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5D.

claim: When the minar2fs139 mutant is treated with U18666A, the cholesterol levels and the AM1-43 labeling intensities are further reduced to significantly lower levels than those in the U18666A-treated wild-type controls.
source: When the minar2fs139 mutant was treated with U18666A, the cholesterol levels and the AM1-43 labeling intensities were further reduced to significantly lower levels than those in the U18666A-treated wild-type controls (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: There is an additive effect between the U18666A treatment and the minar2fs139 mutation.
source: Thus, there was an additive effect between the U18666A treatment and the minar2fs139 mutation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined effects shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Both 2HPβCD and U18666A cause small reductions in hair cell numbers in wild-type controls.
source: The results showed both 2HPβCD and U18666A caused small reductions in hair cell numbers in wild-type controls, but only U18666A further reduced the numbers of hair cells in the neuromasts of mutant minar2fs139 larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by hair cell counting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only U18666A further reduces the numbers of hair cells in the neuromasts of mutant minar2fs139 larvae.
source: The results showed both 2HPβCD and U18666A caused small reductions in hair cell numbers in wild-type controls, but only U18666A further reduced the numbers of hair cells in the neuromasts of mutant minar2fs139 larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by hair cell counting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Efavirenz consistently increases cholesterol levels in neuromast hair cells.
source: We found that efavirenz consistently increased cholesterol levels in the neuromast hair cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by D4H-mCherry measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Treating wild-type larvae with efavirenz causes small increases in D4H-mCherry signals and AM1-43 labeling in neuromast hair cells.
source: We observed that treating the wild-type larvae with efavirenz caused small increases in D4H-mCherry signals (111.2 ± 11.2% of controls, p=0.807) and AM1-43 labeling (107.4 ± 3.6% of controls, p=0.400) in neuromast hair cells, likely because the cholesterol homeostasis mechanism was intact in the wild type.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: After treatment with efavirenz, there are significant increases of D4H-mCherry signals in the hair bundles of the 5 dpf minar2fs139 mutant.
source: In contrast, after treatment with efavirenz, there were significant increases of D4H-mCherry signals in the hair bundles (Figure 6A, from 55.8±7.0%–88.7 ± 8.4% of those of controls, p=0.021), increases of AM1-43 labeling in hair cells in the 5 dpf minar2fs139 mutant (Figure 6B, from 61.8±2.9%–96.1 ± 3.1% of those of controls, p<0.0001), and both were restored to the levels observed in the wild type controls (p=0.269 and p=0.115).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 6A.

claim: After treatment with efavirenz, there are increases of AM1-43 labeling in hair cells in the 5 dpf minar2fs139 mutant.
source: In contrast, after treatment with efavirenz, there were significant increases of D4H-mCherry signals in the hair bundles (Figure 6A, from 55.8±7.0%–88.7 ± 8.4% of those of controls, p=0.021), increases of AM1-43 labeling in hair cells in the 5 dpf minar2fs139 mutant (Figure 6B, from 61.8±2.9%–96.1 ± 3.1% of those of controls, p<0.0001), and both were restored to the levels observed in the wild type controls (p=0.269 and p=0.115).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Efavirenz treatment restores D4H-mCherry signals and AM1-43 labeling to the levels observed in wild type controls.
source: In contrast, after treatment with efavirenz, there were significant increases of D4H-mCherry signals in the hair bundles (Figure 6A, from 55.8±7.0%–88.7 ± 8.4% of those of controls, p=0.021), increases of AM1-43 labeling in hair cells in the 5 dpf minar2fs139 mutant (Figure 6B, from 61.8±2.9%–96.1 ± 3.1% of those of controls, p<0.0001), and both were restored to the levels observed in the wild type controls (p=0.269 and p=0.115).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Treatment with efavirenz rescues the abnormally enlarged vesicles seen in the 8 dpf minar2fs139 mutant.
source: We also found the treatment with efavirenz rescued the abnormally enlarged vesicles seen in the 8 dpf minar2fs139 mutant (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The decreased AM1-43 labeling is reversed after voriconazole treatment.
source: We further tested voriconazole, another CYP46A1 inhibitor, and observed that the decreased AM1-43 labeling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and the abnormal distribution of D4H-mCherry (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) were similarly reversed after the voriconazole treatments.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The abnormal distribution of D4H-mCherry is reversed after voriconazole treatment.
source: We further tested voriconazole, another CYP46A1 inhibitor, and observed that the decreased AM1-43 labeling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and the abnormal distribution of D4H-mCherry (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) were similarly reversed after the voriconazole treatments.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The compromised short-latency C-start (SLC) response rates in the minar2fs139 mutant are rescued to levels in wild-type controls with efavirenz treatment.
source: We found that the compromised short-latency C-start (SLC) response rates in the minar2fs139 mutant were rescued to levels in the wild-type controls with the efavirenz treatment (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by C-start response data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Both mechanotransduction (AM1-43 staining) and hearing are restored after the decreased cholesterol levels are restored by treatment with efavirenz.
source: Thus, both the mechanotransduction (AM1-43 staining) and the hearing were restored after the decreased cholesterol levels were restored by the treatment with efavirenz.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue effects shown in Figure 6B and 6D.

claim: Three CRAC (and its analog CARC) motifs are identified in the primary sequences of Minar2 orthologs.
source: We identified three CRAC (and its analog CARC) motifs in the primary sequences of Minar2 orthologs (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Point mutations of critical aromatic residues (Y/F/W) within CRAC/CARC motifs to alanine should compromise the association between Minar2 and cholesterol.
source: We reasoned that if Minar2 interacted with cholesterol directly with the CRAC/CARC motif, point mutations of the critical aromatic residues (Y/F/W) within these motifs to alanine residues (Fantini et al., 2016; Li and Papadopoulos, 1998; Paschkowsky et al., 2018) should compromise the association between Minar2 and cholesterol.
evidence: This claim is based on reasoning from known properties of CRAC/CARC motifs supported by citations.

claim: The point mutation of MINAR2YW-A compromises the recruitment of cholesterol to the perinuclear region.
source: We observed that the point mutation of MINAR2YW-A compromised the recruitment of cholesterol to the perinuclear region (decreased from 24.58±1.30 au in the MINAR21-190 group to 14.85±0.90 au in the MINAR2YW-A group, p<0.0001) and the intensity of intracellular cholesterol labeling (from 103.9±4.86 au in the MINAR21-190 group to 86.43±3.21 au in the MINAR2YW-A group, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by filipin staining quantification shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The point mutation of MINAR2YW-A compromises the intensity of intracellular cholesterol labeling.
source: We observed that the point mutation of MINAR2YW-A compromised the recruitment of cholesterol to the perinuclear region (decreased from 24.58±1.30 au in the MINAR21-190 group to 14.85±0.90 au in the MINAR2YW-A group, p<0.0001) and the intensity of intracellular cholesterol labeling (from 103.9±4.86 au in the MINAR21-190 group to 86.43±3.21 au in the MINAR2YW-A group, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by filipin staining quantification shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The point mutation construct is expressed at a similar level as the wild-type construct.
source: These effects were not due to changes in expression levels of the point mutation construct, since it was expressed at a similar level as the wild-type construct (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The docking site with the best binding free energy (–8.1 kJ/mol) for cholesterol is located in the conserved sequence pattern that matches the CSD of caveolin.
source: We found the docking site with the best binding free energy (–8.1 kJ/mol) for cholesterol was indeed located in the conserved sequence pattern that matched the CSD of caveolin, and the mutated aromatic residues (W112 and Y117) above were involved in the interaction between Minar2 and cholesterol (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational docking analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mutated aromatic residues (W112 and Y117) are involved in the interaction between Minar2 and cholesterol.
source: We found the docking site with the best binding free energy (–8.1 kJ/mol) for cholesterol was indeed located in the conserved sequence pattern that matched the CSD of caveolin, and the mutated aromatic residues (W112 and Y117) above were involved in the interaction between Minar2 and cholesterol (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational docking analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Kiaa1024L/Minar2 protein, located on the apical endo-membranes and stereocilia membranes, is responsible for the apical distribution of cholesterol to the hair bundle.
source: Our results suggest that the Kiaa1024L/Minar2 protein, located on the apical endo-membranes and stereocilia membranes, is responsible for the apical distribution of cholesterol to the hair bundle, and this apical distribution of cholesterol is essential for the normal morphogenesis and function of the hair bundle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of localization, cholesterol distribution, and mutant phenotypes.

claim: The apical distribution of cholesterol is essential for the normal morphogenesis and function of the hair bundle.
source: Our results suggest that the Kiaa1024L/Minar2 protein, located on the apical endo-membranes and stereocilia membranes, is responsible for the apical distribution of cholesterol to the hair bundle, and this apical distribution of cholesterol is essential for the normal morphogenesis and function of the hair bundle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results showing hair bundle defects when cholesterol distribution is disrupted.

claim: Loss of minar2 markedly reduces cholesterol distribution in the hair bundles.
source: Consistent with this model, loss of minar2 markedly reduces cholesterol distribution in the hair bundles, causes longer and thinner hair bundles, and gives rise to enlarged and aggregated apical lysosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by D4H-mCherry measurements shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Loss of minar2 causes longer and thinner hair bundles.
source: Consistent with this model, loss of minar2 markedly reduces cholesterol distribution in the hair bundles, causes longer and thinner hair bundles, and gives rise to enlarged and aggregated apical lysosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by phalloidin staining measurements shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Loss of minar2 gives rise to enlarged and aggregated apical lysosomes.
